Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

vignette: Lucas Vance stood at the helm of the cutwater 47, the salt-stung air of the marina doing little to clear the haze that had settled over his quarters. At twenty-nine, he had spent most of his adult life navigating coastlines and responding to emergencies, but the incident on the service road behind the naval supply depot had left him adrift in his own life. It had happened on a Tuesday, just past dusk. A man in a dark jacket had stepped from the shadows, a knife catching the last amber light of the setting sun before pressing against Lucas’s ribs. There had been no warning, only the sharp gasp of the robber demanding his wallet and watch, the cold metallic bite of the blade, and the sudden, terrifying realization that his training offered no leverage in a confined, dimly lit space. When the man finally fled, Lucas had stood frozen until the footsteps faded, the silence of the suburban street amplifying the collapse of his sense of security. In the weeks that followed, the event refused to settle into a coherent narrative. Instead, it fractured into isolated shards that arrived without warning. A sudden metallic snap from a fellow crewmate’s duffel bag on the deck became his first true trigger, the sharp sound echoing the robber’s quick movement in the dimly lit alley. His mind drifted to the dark space, pulling disjointed flashes of asphalt and shadow that refused to align into a sequence. He could not put the frightening event into words; attempts to describe it to his partner, Clara, always dissolved into silence, leaving him to stare at his hands as if trying to reconstruct a map that kept tearing apart. On the rare occasions he managed to recall the encounter, the feeling of threat was entirely absent. He would sit in the quiet of his garage, tracing the outline of the stolen watch, and realize he felt completely numb, as if he were reading a police report about someone else, the emotional stakes drained from the moment. He had come to structure his days around the quiet avoidance of certain spaces. He no longer took the service road, choosing instead to drive the longer coastal route even when the tide was turning, and he avoided the dimly lit loading docks where supply trucks idled. The distance was not calculated; it was a slow, automatic drift that had accumulated over months, reshaping his routine until his workdays felt like a series of guarded movements. He remained at the station, his uniform hanging heavy on his shoulders, but the camaraderie that once anchored him had grown thin. Clara noticed the quiet, the way he would sit motionless in the passenger seat during weekend drives, his gaze fixed on the road rather than her, yet he could not explain the weight of it. By the fourth month, the exhaustion of carrying the unprocessed fragments had become its own kind of threat. He found himself seeking help, not because he could articulate what was wrong, but because the silence was no longer bearable. What frightened him most was the fear that he would spend the rest of his life waiting for a memory to make sense, or worse, to feel like his own. He hoped a clinician might help him piece the fragments together, not to relive the violence, but to finally understand why the event refused to stay buried, and to find a way to step back into the light without bracing for the dark.
